So Long, Salon. We’ll Miss You
The publication’s legacy, as told to us by its editors and writers
November 12, 2026
So Long, Salon. We’ll Miss You
The publication’s legacy, as told to us by its editors and writers
STUDY HALL COURSES:
▶ Pitch Workshop: Master the Art of Storytelling
In this live Study Hall
course
, Adam Popescu — a narrative journalist and author whose work has appeared in The New York Times, Bloomberg, and many other outlets — will cover everything from identifying stories to securing assignments. This workshop will focus on pitching (so bring your pitches!) and cover what it takes to succeed in the competitive world of freelance journalism using practical tips and techniques that have helped him build a career at some of the world's most prestigious publications. There will also be a Q&A with Adam at the end of the course.
The 1.5-hour
course
will take place
Monday, November 16th, at 10 AM / 1 PM ET
. The standard price is $99. Study Hall members can use the discount code “studyhallmember” to bring the price to $49.50. For any questions, email
support@studyhall.xyz
.
So Long, Salon. We’ll Miss You
By Carina Imbornone
Share on
X
, Share on
Bluesky
On November 5, after 31 years in business, the pioneering news site
Salon
announced it would cease publication that same day. The history of the digital outlet tracks the history of the World Wide Web. For every trend in digital publishing, you can bet that
Salon
tried it, from digital ads, to moderated comments sections, to
cryptocurrency-mining-as-ad-block-alternative
.
From culture-junkie roots, the online magazine’s editors launched a nimble, politically progressive news organization that helped influence the internet’s role as a public sphere. It produced some of the key cultural-political stories and packages of the 2000s and 2010s, like the post-9/11
“war reader”
, a syllabus on Afghanistan and Osama bin Laden compiled by Anthony York, and Steve Kornacki’s earnest
coming out story
. In 1998, the online site published a major scoop detailing how House Judiciary Committee Chairman Henry Hyde, who played a central role in the impeachment of former President Bill Clinton, had an extramarital affair in the 1960s. There was, well, also that Jake Tapper “
Gangbanging in media land” piece
. Writers like Tapper, Glenn Greenwald, Joan Walsh, and Michelle Goldberg passed through the
Salon
parlor room before becoming the pillars of the media world that we know them to be.
Ultimately, the site succumbed to “business realities of independent digital journalism,” according to a farewell note on the homepage that is signed simply “Salon.” The magazine’s publishing model, which included revenue with advertising and paid subscriptions, was no longer sustainable.
Find.co
, a cryptocurrency marketing company, had purchased
Salon
for an undisclosed sum in November 2023 from Chris Richmond and Drew Schoentrup, who had previously paid $5 million for the publication in August 2019.
To remember
Salon
’s legacy, I spoke to folks whose experience spanned 1995 to 2026: co-founder Scott Rosenberg; Joel Whitney, author of
The Paris Review-CIA exclusive
; Annemarie Dooling, 2010s comments section pioneer; and arts critic Coleman Spilde.
These interviews have been edited and condensed for clarity.
Scott Rosenberg was part of the crew of editors and writers with alt-weekly roots who founded
Salon
in 1995. Before
Salon
, he worked at the
San Francisco Examiner
with David Talbot and several other founders. He also was an early adopter of personal website publishing. He helped launch the site and worked at the publication for the next decade. In his time, he saw the internet grow up and digital media transform. There was even talk, he said, at one point, of a
Salon
cruise, à la
The Nation cruise
, but as far as he could remember, a hurricane put a stop to the plan.
Scott Rosenberg:
Almost all of the founders were people who had worked at the
San Francisco Examiner
. During the newspaper strike in San Francisco in 1994, we put out what was called a strike paper, a daily news website that we produced while on strike. When we went back to our jobs, our editors at the
Examiner
were vindictive. My colleague, David Talbot, always wanted to start a magazine. But no one was putting money into a new general interest magazine, even, you know, 30 years ago. He pivoted and said, well, let's do this on the web.
People looked at us like we were crazy, because our jobs were coveted, rare, and union protected. The first year was very touch and go. We had very little revenue. But by 1997, it was clear that we were growing our audience.
The Henry Hyde story marked the moment that we realized that we were really making an impact. In September 1998, a source who knew a woman who had had an affair with then-House Judiciary Committee Chairman Henry Hyde
came to us
. He told us that he had taken the story to all sorts of mainstream news outlets that all turned him away. We had a lot of debates inside our newsroom, and ultimately, collectively, decided that the American people should know that there were people in glass houses throwing stones. The story was a part of the
political dynamic
of the Clinton impeachment saga.
Every year, there was something happening that would make us wonder, would we make it to the next? We IPO’d in 1999, near the peak of the dot-com bubble. At that point, we were a website company. And we actually knew how to build a website, which was not exactly common knowledge at the time. We went public because it was the only way to survive. We needed money, and the market was showering businesses with money. The first investor was Adobe’s venture capital arm. And as it turned out, the money that we took in from the IPO was just enough to help get us through the bust. We speed ran our way through every possible online business model in those years: a membership program, personal ads, display ads, a paywall after 9/11.
All the advertisers disappeared after 9/11, a year and a half after the beginning of the dot-com bust. Our position at
Salon
was a little more heterodox than most publications at that point. We raised a lot of questions that were not popular. A few days after 9/11, we ran a pretty persuasive article that said that we shouldn't be going to
war in Afghanistan
. For better or worse, Talbot was very committed to having lots of different voices in the mix. For a time, we had a conservative columnist, which drove our readers crazy.
We started a program that I ran called Salon Blogs, an early blogging platform in partnership with a software company. In 2002, Julie Powell started a blog on
Salon
where she cooked her way through Julia Child’s cookbook. That inspired the film
Julie & Julia
. This was pre- Facebook. It was a time when the web industry had just coined “user generated content.”
We were much more in charge of our destiny than we had been as employees of newspaper companies, where the business model was set in stone and you were going to ride that stone to the bottom of the ocean as the technology changed. The fact that, you know, we actually built a business that lasted this long is astonishing to me. If you had told me in 1995 that
Salon
would survive for 31 years, I would have been thrilled, but I would have found it absolutely not credible. We tried all these things that later proved to be actually good businesses in various ways, but we were either, you know, premature, or we didn't know how to do it right, or the technology wasn't ready, or it wasn't a big enough audience.
The thing that mattered most to us was that we were publishing really unique voices and people who were a little bit odd. We were not part of New York. We were just a bunch of weirdos in the Bay Area, excited about the chance to post our writing.
Joel Whitney published his
Salon
exclusive
“The Paris Review, the Cold War, and the CIA”
in 2012. His reporting revealed that the magazine’s editors, including George Plimpton, sought ties to the Congress for Cultural Freedom, a covert anti-communist
CIA operation
. The story built on other reporting about
connections
between
The Paris Review
and the CIA. The piece was Whitney’s first in which the source died, he said, and his first time going viral.
Joel Whitney:
It started as a story about Barney Rosset, the rebel publisher who founded
The Evergreen Review
and was the owner of Grove Press. I wanted to write about Rosset because I got an unverified tip that Rosset had been approached by the editors of
The Paris Review
to publish writers who were a part of the non-Communist Left, which is what the CIA's Congress for Cultural Freedom
was into
.
Rosset apparently declined. When I heard about this, I immediately emailed Rosset, I think on a Sunday night, and he agreed to an interview on Wednesday morning. But by Tuesday
he was dead
. So I went to
The Paris Review
archives and I found the story.
As a freelancer, the relationship with
Salon
was key. My editor, Dave Daley, was just so supportive.
Salon
helped pioneer the idea that people want to sit down on web-only platforms and read things that make you a better citizen. Dave told me he thought the story would have a “long tail.” He was the first editor to teach me the phrase.
Being an MFA brat coming out of Columbia University, I wanted to write about the cross section between art and politics.
Salon
pioneered the space between pop culture, high culture, anti-war, and left progressive politics. At their best, that's what culture and literary magazines do.
The thing that always stuck with me was showing that you could push back against legacy media from the left. You can be clear on your anti-war progressive values.
Salon
was one of the places that I saw at the cutting edge of that.
Annemarie Dooling
joined
Salon
in 2014 to help build the community section of the site, a moderated comments section where readers could engage with fellow readers and the site’s writers. She went on to become the vice president of audience growth and experiences at
USA Today,
and now works for
News Creator Corps
, a program for creators to produce digital stories that empower communities with information and resources. She also runs
The Platia
, her own micro newsroom, which connects readers with mutual aid opportunities in Philadelphia.
Annemarie Dooling:
It was 24/7. I was moderating comments all day. We felt like we had to be online constantly. People didn't bring their laptops home from work before that.
Salon
had hundreds and hundreds of commenters who were very interested in chatting with the writers. Back then, people weren't chatting on social media that much. And so people were leaving comments on news sites. We realized that that was a separate business in itself. We were definitely the best at moderation. We blocked the trolls.
I monitored the comments for
Salon’s
TV and film writing. Content about film and TV really bonds people. You can have nothing else in common, but you can both love a TV show. The writers were very involved in their communities. They knew commenters' names.
I sometimes wonder if we made an error opening the floodgates and telling everyone that they should say things all the time on the internet. And I mean, this didn't happen right away. At the time, we elevated a commenter because they have lived experience in television or they had knowledge we don't have. And then that sort of moderation stopped, people stopped paying for that. And so then everyone's opinion truly became equal. There's no hierarchy. There's no expertise.
And I'm one of the people that championed the open internet, right? I willingly architected the internet we have now. But sometimes I feel sort of like the guy who made the office cubicle.
Do you know the story about the guy who invented the cubicle? He lived the rest of his life in
regret
. And sometimes I feel like that.
Coleman Spilde was part of the last masthead of
Salon
. As senior culture writer and critic at
Salon
, he covered film. Previously, he worked as a staff critic at
The Daily Beast
, and his work has appeared in
Vulture
and
Slate
. He’s now at work on a novel and open for new opportunities. Working at
Salon
was a unicorn of a job, he said, even though he got a lot of email inquiries from confused folks asking where to get a haircut.
Coleman Spilde
:
At
Salon
, there was always an emphasis on making sure that arts and culture were in conversation with politics. A lot of the work that we ended up trying to do was take a very liberal audience and keep pushing them to the left by asking tougher questions. We were very scrappy. We knew that we had to throw some punches here and there. I think our senior politics writer,
Amanda Marcotte
, was so good at that. She has such a strong feminist, progressive voice that offered so many solutions.
The end was truly like those horror stories that you read about. We all got a Slack message to join a meeting with the general manager and the parent company. And I was like, “oh, the bottom has fallen out and we're all about to get the axe.” I think maybe it was like four people had their cameras on to start, and by the end, I'm pretty sure almost all of them were off. We got to spend the rest of the day commiserating and celebrating together, which was really, really wonderful because I think so much of the experience of being at
Salon
was having such incredible, supportive, kind colleagues who truly were there for you.
It was such a small team that we knew we had to help each other out in any way that we could. So when the blow came down, it was a lot of us just being like, “man, we fought so fucking hard, but it just wasn't enough.” We had felt like we were starting to make gains and see the business turn around and see traffic boosting. And it just wasn't enough time to turn it all around in the way that the owners would have liked to see.
The owners, from what I knew, really, really believed in us. It was a site of voices. They weren't so concerned about a consistent editorial voice. That’s what made it so interesting and fun to read. I think you could go to our site and you wouldn't know entirely what to expect. The angles were always sharp and very voice-forward. You just see that less and less in journalism. It really was important for us to always be asking more questions than answers, and then providing answers. We really considered it our place to look at the world as it is and be really honest. We pitched stories by asking questions like, “does this make me believe that the world can be a better place?” “Can I make the reader think twice about something?”
We're all just trying to make sense of a very chaotic, scary, tough world.
Salon
is a seismic loss.
Interview with Eve Sneider
On the latest Study Hall Podcast
episode
, Eve Sneider discussed her new book
The Absent Woman: The Genius of Janet Malcolm
. Sneider talked about how Janet Malcolm’s writing foreshadowed Nathan Fielder’s
You Can See Everything
, and what contemporary writers can learn from Malcolm’s deconstructive approach to reporting.
Listen
here
.
